title: On Gender
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk highlights the importance of addressing gender dynamics in Zen practice to prevent similar situations from arising, particularly when charismatic leaders become seduced by power and engage in addictive behavior. This issue is not new, but rather a manifestation of societal conditioning that can lead to prejudice against women, emphasizing the need for embracing our differences rather than trying to suppress them. By recognizing and respecting the complexity and nuance of human experience, including gender and consent, we can cultivate true loving-kindness and enlightenment.

sentences.text: Dear visitors, I forgot you were coming today.
I hope that what I have to say is of some use to you, maybe not.
Hi Dan, it's been a while.
How are you?
Well, I had such a good time yesterday listening to Tim's talk.
Thank you, that was thrilling.
It was, I was thrilled.
I think it was wonderful, I'm thankful.
So now I'm kind of charged up to hear Edie's talk this afternoon; it's got me going.
Edie told me she has a very interesting subject, and I'm just Edie's worm on that.
So, anyway, what fun, what a great thing.
And I actually had planned on speaking about something that Tim brought up yesterday.
I wanted to go into some more detail about it.

It's not the kind of thing I usually talk about, but I would like to speak about it because I don't know how many of you follow these things on the internet, but he mentioned this yesterday, all this discussion in the national Zen community about sexual misconduct by the male Zen teachers.
And so I want to talk a little bit about that, and I'll tell you who the teachers were.

They were Eido Shimano, who's a Rinzai Zen master from Japan, a Japanese guy who in the seventies founded Dai Bosatsu Monastery in upstate New York and has been teaching there and in New York City for all these years, and Gempo Merzel, who's an American guy who was an early disciple of Maezumi Roshi, a very powerful person who founded a number of Zen centers both here and extensively in Europe.
The sort of seat of the whole outfit is in Salt Lake City.
Gempo also is the creator of something called the Big Mind Process, which is a kind of quasi-Zen psychological training that he's been spending more and more time on in recent years.
So Gempo is maybe in his late sixties, a few years older than me, and Shimano is about a decade older than that.
Both of them are really charismatic, powerful Zen masters, powerful in their ability to project a sense of Zen understanding of life.
And both of them, I mean, I know Gempo fairly well, I don't know Shimano, but both of them probably are troubled by some form of sexual addiction.
They have some problems, I think.
So this is now, because of the Internet, it's really big news, but unfortunately it's very old news.
We've seen this before, too many times before, from these very same people and from others.
We've seen it in Zen, we've seen it in other forms of Buddhism, we've seen it in other religions, we've seen it in outside of religion, in the secular world.
And it seems like I'm getting the impression, over the years, that there's some kind of syndrome or something.
Like people who are in the business of diagnosing mental illness usually are seeing people who have, they're not seeing powerful people, right?
So they haven't named this syndrome because they don't see, their patients are not powerful people, so they don't get to identify.

But I think among powerful people there's a kind of syndrome going on here, which is particularly affects charismatic and powerful, particularly male, spiritual teachers—some kind of seduction and addiction, and who knows why or where this comes from.
And we rightly condemn those actions because they're so blind and so hurtful and they can be devastating in a community as we've seen.
And there really is no excuse or any mitigating circumstances.

At the same time, I can really appreciate how someone could be quite destabilized without realizing that he has become destabilized by the pressures of being a spiritual leader at the head of a community.
I can really get that.
People think it must be glorious to be a spiritual leader, but actually it's no picnic; it's actually kind of hard.

And the better you are at it and the more it seems like you're on top of things and all wise and all powerful and everything you say is right and everybody obeys and agrees, the more crazy making and difficult the situation can become, and you don't realize it.
So being enlightened and always having the controlling viewpoint can literally make you crazy.
And you don't realize you're crazy, and it can make you do very irrational things.
You think to yourself, how could somebody do this?
I mean, I said this to Gempo years ago because he did it before.
I said, Gempo, seeing the things that happen, knowing that you never get away with this, how in the world could you do this?
And basically, he said in so many words, I can't help myself.
You do irrational things.
Look at Mr.
Qaddafi in Libya; it's a crazy thing.
So what do you say when something like this happens in the Zen community?
It's really painful and sad.
But now it's different now.
And as Tim was saying, thank goodness Zen teachers from all around the country get active.
And many of us, myself included, sent letters to the boards of directors of the centers where these teachers taught.
And we said to the boards of directors, these people should not teach.
They should be kicked out of the center.
They shouldn't be kicked upstairs either; they should be gone.
And I think our letters helped, and in fact, that happened.
In both these cases, both these teachers left their communities, were asked to leave.
In one case, Shimano was asked to leave.
Gempo, under the pressure, withdrew himself.
And in both cases, there were successor teachers who could step in.
And the national community of Zen teachers expressed support for these successor teachers.
And I think that, I don't know how, it must be quite difficult, but I think there's a possibility anyway that the communities could really survive this disaster.
This is so much better than years ago when stuff like this would happen and there was no real support or understandable way of dealing with it, so it was more difficult.
Still though, I think that both Shimano and Gempo will continue teaching, not in those centers, but somehow in other ways.
As long as people want to go to them, attracted by their power, they will continue teaching.
And no one can really stop them until someone actually takes them to court, which probably will happen at some point.
And take them to court and sue them, and somehow prevent them from continuing.
From what I can tell, Shimano is completely unrepentant.
I mean, I'm not so close to the situation, but it looks like that.
And Gempo seems to be repentant, but one has to be suspicious because both these teachers have a long history of this conduct, over more than twenty-five years.
So one can't be naive, as we know for ourselves, it's hard to change, very hard to change.
So we have to have low expectations and be realistic.
Anyway, actually that's not what I want to talk about today because it seems to me that we all know better than this.
And I don't think that this sort of thing is something we've ever had to deal with in our sanghas, at least so far.
Let's hope for the future that we don't have to deal with it.

And I'm pretty sure that if we ever had somebody around in our sanghas, whether it was a teacher or not a teacher, who was this kind of a person, I don't think that that guy would last very long before people were saying to him, "Well, wait a minute here.
Straighten out, buster.
You can't be doing this."
Certainly the women in our sanghas, I don't think, would be fooled by this for a moment.
So I'm not that worried about it, actually.
And I don't so much feel like it's an issue for us, nor do I feel like it's something that I have to comment on or diagnose anybody or condemn anybody.
I feel sorry, actually, for everybody involved.
So that's not actually what I want to talk about.
But I want to talk about something more subtle that this reminds me of, and that's why I bring it up in the beginning.

Something that we never talk about because it actually never comes up in the traditional teachings, but it does exist, and it is an important issue for us, and that is gender dynamics in our practice.

Now, in talking about this, I'm not trying to say something definitive because I think that this is an issue on which there is almost nothing definitive that anybody can say, because no one is free of gender bias.
There's nobody outside of gender history looking at it as if they were from Mars.
So we're all prisoners of our conditioning.
So I'm not trying to say anything definitive or important other than just to speak about it by way of opening up the subject.

And though, as I say, I'm pretty sure that sexual predation is not a big factor in our song of life, probably gender dynamics is, and it's very hard to talk about this stuff because as soon as you open up your mouth, it stirs deep feelings in all of us.
And we talked about it quite a bit in our song at home in everyday Zen in the Bay Area.
We actually had a month of the seminar or so, which we called Women in Buddhism, and we raised these questions and issues of gender.
And it was not that easy, it turns out, not so easy.
Are you looking for a place to sit?
I think there's some spots there in the back.
So we had good conversations, and we tried hard, but it was not the most comfortable and happy-making month of our Dharma seminar.
At the end, I said at the end, "Well, how did this go?"
And people said, "Well, I don't know if I liked it that much."
But it's not that comfortable to talk about this stuff, actually.
It sort of puts all of us on edge.
And I don't want to make you feel uncomfortable in what I want to say, and even more than that, I don't want to be uncomfortable.
So I'll try to say things that are more on the comfortable side, if possible.
So, as many of you here know, Florence Caplow and Sue Moon have been collecting women's Zen and Buddhist stories for a book they're proposing to do.
And they were actually up here in the Northwest doing a weekend, which I think had a big impact that people really enjoyed on those stories.
So they've sent me some of the material they have.
And I don't know all the stories, but I've looked into this before, and I'm familiar with many of them, and I look forward to looking more closely at their materials.
But most of the stories that involve women don't necessarily involve gender issues.
You wouldn't know; it doesn't make any difference in a lot of the stories whether it's a woman or a man.
And that's as it should be.
Questions of truth are questions of truth, and it doesn't matter if it's a man or woman or male truth or female truth; it really doesn't matter.
But sometimes it does matter.
And sometimes we see the difference between a male truth and a female truth, and sometimes through this difference, wider truths emerge.
So one of the stories in their collection, which I've seen before, and I don't know, I may have talked about this before, this particular story really does focus on gender issues.
And Every Day's End in the Bay Area also has an annual women's retreat.
And this year they focused on this story, and they even dramatized it.
They enacted the story.
And Chris Forten, one of our senior priests down there, and Sue Moon and others actually played out this koan, this story, like a little drama.
So here's the story.
Kind of an amazing story, actually.
Wanan was the senior monk at Dahui's monastery.
Dahui was a Song dynasty, very famous teacher, and so Song dynasty a little later than most of the stories.
Anyway, Wanan was the head monk there, and Dahui had seven women disciples.
And Miaozong was the most beautiful of the seven.
Miaozong became a nun, but before she became a nun, she would come to practice with Dahui, and he would put her up in the abbot's quarters.
And the head monk Wanan always made disapproving noises about this.
And Dahui said to him, even though she is a woman, she has strengths.
Wanan did not approve of this at all.
So Dahui then insisted that he should interview her, and Wanan didn't want to do it, but finally he agreed.
And he sent a message, "We'll talk."
So Miaozong first said to him, "Will this be a Dharma interview or a worldly interview?"
Wanan replied, "A Dharma interview."
Miaozong then said to him, "Then let your attendance go," and she went into the room first.
A little moment passed and she said, "Please come in."
When he walked in past the curtain, he saw Miaozong lying face upward on a bed without anything on at all, naked.
Kind of startling.
But Wanan was a very self-possessed Zen guy.
So he walked in, pointed to her genitals and said, "What kind of place is this?"
And Miaozong replied, "All the Buddhas of the three worlds and the six patriarch's and all the great monks everywhere come from here."
Wanan then said, "And would you let me enter or not?"
Miaozong replied, "Horses cross, asses cannot cross."
This finally left Wanan speechless.
And Miaozong said to him, "The interview is over."
And she turned over and Wanan, very embarrassed, left the room, went back to Dahui, and Dahui said to him, "It is certainly not the case that the old dragon does not have any insight."
And the story ends, Wanan was ashamed.
A pretty provocative story.
Miaozong confronts these gender issues head on and nakedly, so to speak.
Now it looks like this head monk, Wanan, unlike our head monk who has been around the block a few times and has some wisdom and seen some things, is not so easily scandalized, I would imagine.
But Wanan is easily scandalized or is scandalized by the idea of a woman staying in the monastery in the abbot's quarters.
And in reality, these sorts of things that we were talking about in the beginning are not news from yesterday or news from a decade or two ago.

There are news from the ages because even in this time in the Song dynasty, Dahui's teacher, Yuanwu, who was the monk who compiled the Blue Cliff record, he was known to have had many illicit affairs and he would house the women in his monastery, which is why perhaps Wanan, the head monk, was suspicious of this.
So he, I guess, assumes that Miaozong is a woman like that and she has no business being in the monastery.
And think about it, maybe if we were around we would be just like him, right?
This is wrong, this is scandalous, this is a violation of ethical conduct.
And we too would have been suspicious.
But it may be also that Wanan is also beyond worried about ethical conduct, maybe a little prejudiced against women.
Maybe he's a little patronizing.
How could a woman with a woman's body and a woman's point of view really penetrate the Dharma, he might have thought.
He doesn't really want to talk to her about this; he just wants her to go away.
And Dahui realizes that it's much better for him not to defend her but to let her defend herself, and she seems more than capable of doing this.

So probably, if we're honest, we would have to say that there's no way to pretend when there are men and women involved practicing together, as we do, which when the Japanese see this they cannot imagine how it's possible.
Probably there's no way to pretend that when there's men and women together that there's no sexual energy.
There's always sexual energy and other kinds of gender-influenced energies, like fear or resentment.
So Wanan knows this and he would like to be protected from it.
He would like to remove these energies from the premises, as if he could.
And certainly Miaozong could have pleaded with him that she was now a nun, she was now committed to chastity and obedience, and therefore she was no threat to him or any other men in the monastery.
She could easily have said that and maybe he would have been satisfied.
But that's not what she does.
Instead she confronts the issue with great courage and directness, not apologizing for her feminine body, but emphasizing it.
It is this very femininity, this very womb, that is the source of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, she tells him.
The feminine in all its starkness is not to be finessed or put up with.
It's not a side road, she's telling him; it is the main road.
Everyone passes through here.
It's wonderful to me that Miaozong fearlessly bears her female body, as if to say, "Okay, have a look, this is me.
This is the female form with all of its mystery, all of its beauty, and all of its frightfulness.
This is what you're afraid of.
This is what you doubt.
Take a good look."
She's saying, "It's just me, an ordinary woman.
And it's much more than this.
It's the Tathagatagarbha, the womb of all the Buddhas, the source of enlightenment, the Buddha nature itself."
That's what Buddha nature is.
Tathagatagarbha, which translates literally as womb of all the Buddhas.
When we talk about Buddha nature, that's what we're talking about.
This womb is the essential heart of our practice.
It's what we rely on and have confidence in.
The pain of gender is not to be transcended or sidestepped.
It itself is the Buddha way.
And we sit, we practice hard for three days sitting here.
Not to get something we don't have, not to get some relief we're seeking, not to become something that we're not.
We sit here because we have confidence in this womb of all the Buddhas, in this Buddha nature—the basic brightness of what we already are.
No matter what we are, whether we're a man or a woman, good or bad, skillful or not skillful, or good meditators or bad meditators, it makes no difference.
We are alive.
We are human.
We are embodied as Miaozong is, and we've all come from the great womb of all the Buddhas.
This is most essentially what we are, and this is the mysterious love that sustains us and holds us in its embrace, sitting with confidence in that, returning to that, cutting through our confusion.
That's our practice; this is our zazen.
Miaozong is letting this unfortunately limited head monk know that he should not be denying and protecting himself from what he fears and doesn't understand.
She is telling him that this energy—this sexual energy, this energy of gender, this female energy—is essential to true and profound loving-kindness.
Without this connecting warmth, there is no compassion and there is no enlightenment.
Unfortunately, Mr.
Wanan misses this point at the beginning anyway.
He must have thought at first that somehow Miaozong is offering herself to him.
I was right; he fails to pay attention to what she says to him.
He doesn't see the Tathagatagarbha in the body in front of him; instead, he sees what he suspected, the body of an alluring courtesan.

It's not clear to me in the story, probably it doesn't really matter, but it's not clear to me whether Wanan has been so undone by her beauty that he throws his monk's chastity out the window and he actually is dying to have relations with her, or whether he's just challenging her in some way.
Anyway, you can't fool around with Miaozong.
To Wanan's inquiry, "Can I enter?" she says, "Horses cross, asses do not cross."
This is a wonderful response, of course, and there's a little background to it, which I'll tell you.
It refers to another story that I have to tell you so that you can appreciate.
This is a story about Zhaozhou, who I always talk about because I love Zhaozhou, and what I love about him is that he was so unimpressive.
Maybe he's the least impressive of all the Zen masters.
Or another way of putting it, he was incredibly impressive exactly because he was so unimpressive.
From what we know about him, it would appear that he was not too charismatic or enlightened, and yet he did become well-known for his teaching.
That's why, in the story I'm about to tell you, a monk travels a far distance to go to visit Zhaozhou, and he was very unimpressed.
It's like disappointing to go really far to see a famous Zen master, and here's this shlomil, you know what I mean?
The guy's got nothing going for us.
He came a thousand miles, and this is who I'm visiting?
So there was a famous bridge in the town where Zhaozhou lived, a famous stone bridge of Zhaozhou.
Speaking in code, the monk says to Zhaozhou, "So I came all this way to see the famous stone bridge of Zhaozhou, but all I see is this old log bridge.
Pretty nervy, you know?"
And Zhaozhou says to him, in a very quiet voice, "You can imagine, oh, you see the old log bridge and you don't see the stone bridge."
The monk says, "Well, what is the stone bridge?"
The monk is a little bit taken aback by this, and he says, "Well, what is the stone bridge?"
Zhaozhou says, "Horses cross, asses cross."
It's different from what Miaozong says.
"Horses cross, asses cross."
So horses are the great, powerful Zen students, and asses are the not-so-great and not-so-powerful Zen students.

This monk is coming looking for the charismatic, enlightened, powerful Zen master, and with his eyes blinded by that preconception, he fails to see how big and how all-inclusive this practice actually is.
It's not so small as we're looking for this or we're looking for that; it's much bigger than that.
This is just the same what Tim was referring to yesterday in the story of Nanyay: practice cannot be defiled.
It's all-inclusive.
It cannot be divided.
Yes, it includes the enlightened, that's good, but also it includes the unenlightened.

It includes the impressive and also the not-so-impressive, with the recognition that when it comes to Tathagatagarbha, the difference between the enlightened and the unenlightened and the impressive and the not-impressive is like the difference between blue and red, different colors.
Maybe red is your favorite color, but you would never go on a campaign against blue or say that blue is of much less value than that.
Makes no sense, right?

The more you're looking for the impressive and the charismatic and the enlightened, the more you may be missing it, and incidentally, or maybe not incidentally, the more vulnerable you may be to your own suffering.
In the story, Maitreya is alluding to this saying of Jaja, and of course she gives it a different twist.

She has just demonstrated to one on the all-inclusive nature of her feminine body, and she shows him that her body is not what one saw and thought it was—a sexualized object tempting to others and limited to itself.
The very female form is, as it is, viscerally the Tathagatagarbha, the womb of all Buddhas.
All sentient beings are born from this place, asses and horses alike.
Now she makes a further point: within this limitless feminine form, there are limits.
"Horses cross, asses don't cross."

She's putting our head monk in our proper place, as we could sense even without knowing the background here, and at the same time, she's affirming the power of consent that goes along with the feminine form.
This is the great sorrow and shame of our species because too often throughout history, and even now, even now in so many places, women have been violently robbed of their consent.
They have been raped, they have been demeaned, they have been forced, they have been manipulated into very restricted places.
Miao Zong is saying that the true female form cannot be violated that way; its power of consent is inherent to it.
The womb of the Buddhas issues forth life and shouts its own lion's roar.
The nun, Miao Zong, may be open and yielding and all-inclusive, and yet she alone has the power to say, "Yes, this horse is worthy of me.
No, this ass is not."
The limitless offering of love and warmth and compassion also has its proper limits.
Ethical precepts obtain, even when we hold them limitlessly in a limitless world; we know the difference between something that can be done and something that should not be done.
Miao Zong shows that she has the wisdom and the power to impose those limits herself when it is correct to do so.
So Wanan's worries about her presence in the temple were completely unfounded.
She knew exactly why she was there, and she knew exactly how to conduct herself.

I said before that I believe, and I hope it's true, that in our Sangha male sexual predators don't really exist, and I also hope and believe that narrow-minded, puritanical, possibly misogynistic practitioners don't exist.
But these are extremes.
Between these extremes there's all sorts of subtle confusions and delusions and hurts and pains about gender.

All sorts of ways that probably without any of us intending it, male, unconscious male attitudes are hurtful to women, and perhaps also it goes the other way around: women's attitudes are hurtful to men.
The reason why we don't speak about it much is that none of us can be quite sure about it.
We might have our feelings, but we can't be quite confident that it makes sense to speak of them, and so much of it is unconscious.
We all have family histories; we all have many ways in which we've been conditioned.
Some of us have been hurt or dishonored, and despite our best efforts in practice, we can't help but bring our habits and our wounds and our poor training to our daily conduct.
Sometimes we feel wounded or we inflict wounds without anybody intending for that to happen, but it does happen, and it happens pretty much every day.
It happens not only in Zen places.
It would be nice if it could be restricted to Zen places, and then we could say, "Bring it all here, we'll suffer."
Unfortunately, it's not restricted to Zen places; it's everywhere.
I think we all have to realize that we are very lucky here because in the world that we live in, it's so shockingly different in other parts of the world.
This is, I think, one of the cultural battlegrounds of world culture right now.
But here, it's not so restrictive and so difficult.
There is not what we would call terrible, serious and violent oppression of women here, and of gay and lesbian people, all people, all genders and races.
We don't have that so much here, by and large, at least by comparison; we have an equal chance, and we are all accorded respect, and it's the law here.
It's a blessing; it's the law.
Little by little, it becomes more and more the social custom.
Even here, we're still having our battles over the law and the custom, but even so, there's plenty of hurt and pain, plenty of confusion.
Even when all the hurt and pain is gone, and all the laws provide everyone with freedom and equality, we'll still have the long history of all of this to deal with.
We try our best to bring to awareness what we are unaware of and to follow through our commitment to benefit rather than hurt each other.
In our Soto Zen way of practice, especially in the everyday Zen way, we emphasize warm human relationships.
We emphasize deep trust and mutual commitment, and we honor and give power to senior practitioners.
I think this is a good thing; this is the way that we've inherited, and I think it's a good way.
I personally prefer it to some other way in which what's given credit and power is accomplishment or brilliance or social connection or polish.
Our way is very simple and very warm-hearted.
If you practice, we honor you, we respect you, we love you.
Our way is a way of love.
We grow to accept and love one another in the Dharma as we go forward practicing together, as we were saying yesterday.
We practiced together a long time; we appreciate each other, we accept each other.
We know our foibles, and we don't deny it, but we accept and appreciate.
With this emphasis on love and relationship, there may also be some problems.
People who love one another can misunderstand one another and even hurt one another without intending to do that.
I know that sometimes women have complained about me and other of our male leaders as not really understanding sometimes what a woman is feeling or saying.
I have felt maybe that I misinterpreted or misunderstood or didn't appreciate what is said or what is indicated.

Sometimes women have complained about me or other senior male students saying something or doing something, some word or gesture that maybe in the grand scheme of things is not so bad, but to that person did really matter and was hurtful.
Maybe once or twice we've misunderstood one another so that it seems as if inappropriate relationships are being fostered.
Lots of stuff like this is happening all the time, and we're all, I think, trying to deal with it the best we can, and I think we're doing pretty good.
I think we're pretty mature and understanding and aware people, and I would say that we're doing well.
I don't believe that I have a problem or we have a problem or our other senior teachers have a problem, at least this is my hope.
I hope this is right; somebody after this talk will let me know.
I'm sure I'll hear about that.
That's one reason why I'm saying it; I'm letting you know that I want to hear about it if that's not the case.

That's what I believe anyway, and I'm pretty sure that if I do have a problem or others of us have a problem, that someone will eventually let me or us know, and that we will find a way to deal with it that is open-minded and compassionate.

We don't have to be afraid of problems, and it would be very bad if we were afraid to bring up something that seemed wrong or troubling to us, even if just troubling to me, troubling to an individual.
We need to feel that we can bring it up.
Saying that, I also hasten to say that it would also be fine if you have something that you could easily let go, please let it go.
It would be a rough world if we were all the time, each one of us, letting each other know about all the things that we were saying and doing that were somewhat less than perfectly thoughtful.
I can imagine that if we took up a practice like this, we would have no time to sit; we would have to spend three days in deep conversation about reviewing yesterday's conversation.

One could take this all too far, but still, if it would be good for us, if it would be good for me, and any of our senior teachers, educational for us, to sometimes discuss these things so that we could understand better the different gender dynamics, this would be worthwhile, I think.

The usual way that this is framed is, and I've heard this many times and I don't really disagree, men are so clueless; they really have no interest in and no capacity for feeling anything, whereas women are so much more sensitive and see so much more.
This may very well be true, but also, it may insufficiently take into account the inevitable gender bias that women have, however they come by it, they may have that.
I think the conversation always begins with the realization that we're all a little bit off.
That's what it means to be human with six senses; it means you're always going to be a little bit off, everyone in our own special way, a little bit off.
I'll conclude with some words from Chris, who I was telling you, some of you know Chris Fortin, who she actually said she did not take off all her clothes to enact this.
She put on a body stocking, she said, very, very resourceful.
But at the Women's Retreat, she said that enacting that koan, putting her sort of body into that koan had a big impact on her.
She's still sort of trying to sort out what it meant to her; it was a big deal for her.
She gave a talk about it at the Women's Retreat, so I'll end my talk today with quoting a few paragraphs from her talk.
This is Chris's words:
*The theme for the Every Day Zen Women's Weekend is authentic meeting, ferocious vulnerability.*
Tim was talking quite a bit yesterday about this important study on vulnerability, and that's what they use as a theme for their retreat: vulnerable ferocity.
The dictionary offers us this about the source of these words: Ferocious denotes wild.
Vulnerable is capable of being physically or emotionally wounded, completely seen.
That's interesting, huh?
Capable of being physically or emotionally wounded, completely seen.
Miao Zhang was naked in this encounter.
Nakedness means unarmed, without addition or concealment, nothing extra, bare.
On reflection, this seems to express the heart of the practice that we share with Miao Zhang and all of our ancestors.
Zazen becomes the naked, unarmed, bare act of ferocity: wildly and wholeheartedly committing ourselves to sitting and breathing in the midst of the vulnerable suffering of being a human being.
That's pretty good, huh?
Let me read that sentence again.
Zazen becomes the naked, unarmed, bare act of ferociously, wildly and wholeheartedly committing ourselves to sitting and breathing in the midst of the vulnerable suffering of being a human being.
It is where we meet ourselves and the whole world.

What arises from this practice is a deep confidence and trust that is rooted in the body in everyday activity and in an awareness of the interconnected karmic dance of cause and effect between all beings.
With a faith that makes us vulnerable, that humanizes and connects us, we vow not to turn away from what is uncomfortable.
This is ferocious vulnerability.
Practice awakens our hearts and minds to the wisdom and compassion of the Buddhas.
It cuts through limiting discriminations and self-centered views, the root cause of human suffering.
Talking about these things, there's not much to say in this kind of a forum because most of the talking is very specific between us as human beings.

But I wanted to say something today because of all these things that have been stirring on the Internet, all these reflections, and I've been having many communications—there's a Zen teacher's listserv so that everybody communicates back and forth about these things—and it's been on my mind.
I wanted to say this today.
If this was somehow not relevant to you guys coming from outside today, I would have thought you were coming.
I might have talked about something else, but I forgot.
Keeping Chris's wonderful definition of zazen in mind, I think we can all sit with a lot of appreciation and softness for the rest of our audience for listening.

verbatim.text: Dear visitors, I forgot you were coming today. I hope that what I have to say is of some use to you. Maybe not. Hi Dan. It's been a while. How are you? Well, I had such a good time yesterday listening to Tim's talk. Thank you. That was thrilling. It was. I was thrilled. I think it was wonderful. I'm thankful. So now I'm kind of charged up to hear Edie's talk this afternoon. It's got me going. Edie told me she has a very interesting subject. I'm just Edie's worm on that. Yeah. So, anyway, what fun. What a great thing.

And I actually had planned on speaking about something that Tim brought up yesterday. I wanted to go into some more detail about it. It's not the kind of thing I usually talk about. But I would like to speak about it. Because I don't know how many of you follow these things on the internet, but he mentioned this yesterday, all this discussion in the national Zen community about sexual misconduct by the male Zen teachers. And so I want to talk a little bit about that. And I'll tell you who the teachers were. They were Eido Shimano, who's a Rinzai Zen master from Japan, a Japanese guy who in the 70s founded Dai Bosatsu Monastery in upstate New York and has been teaching there and in New York City for all these years. And Gempo Merzel, who's an American guy who was an early disciple of Maezumi Roshi,

a very powerful person who founded a number of Zen centers both here and extensively in Europe. And the sort of seat of the whole outfit is in Salt Lake City. Gempo also is the creator of something called the Big Mind Process, which is a kind of quasi-Zen psychological training that he's been spending more and more time on in recent years. So Gempo is maybe in his late 60s, a few years older than me, and Shimano is about a decade older than that. And both of them are really charismatic, powerful Zen masters, powerful in their ability to project a sense of Zen understanding of life. And both of them, I mean, I know Gempo fairly well, I don't know Shimano,

but both of them probably are troubled by some form of sexual addiction. They have some problems, I think. So this is now, you know, because of the Internet, it's really big news, but unfortunately it's very old news. We've seen this before, too many times before, from these very same people and from others. We've seen it in Zen, we've seen it in other forms of Buddhism, we've seen it in other religions, we've seen it in outside of religion, in the secular world. And it seems like I'm getting the impression, you know, over the years that there's some kind of syndrome or something. You know, like people who are in the business of diagnosing mental illness,

usually are seeing, you know, people who have, they're not seeing powerful people, right? So they haven't named this syndrome, because they don't see, their patients are not powerful people, so they don't get to identify. But I think among powerful people there's a kind of syndrome going on here, which is particularly, you know, affects charismatic and powerful, particularly male, spiritual teachers, some kind of seduction and addiction and who knows why or where this comes from. And we, you know, we rightly condemn those actions because they're so blind and so hurtful and they can be devastating, you know, in a community as we've seen. And there really is no excuse or any mitigating circumstances.

At the same time, I can really appreciate how someone could be quite destabilized without realizing that he has become destabilized by the pressures of being a spiritual leader at the head of a community. I can really get that. People think, you know, it must be glorious to be a spiritual leader, but actually it's no picnic. It's actually kind of hard. And the better you are at it and the more it seems like you're on top of things and all wise and all powerful and everything you say is right and everybody obeys and agrees, the more crazy making and difficult the situation can become and you don't realize it. So being enlightened and always having the controlling viewpoint can literally make you crazy.

And you don't realize you're crazy. And it can make you do very irrational things. You think to yourself, how could somebody do this? I mean, I said this to Gempo years ago because he did it before. I said, Gempo, seeing the things that happen, knowing that you never get away with this, how in the world could you do this? And basically, I mean, he said in so many words, I can't help myself. You do irrational things. Look at Mr. Qaddafi in Libya. It's a crazy thing. So what do you say when something like this happens in the Zen community? It's really painful and sad. But now it's different now.

And as Tim was saying, thank goodness, Zen teachers from all around the country get active. And many of us, myself included, sent letters to the boards of directors of the centers where these teachers taught. And we said to the boards of directors, these people should not teach. They should be kicked out of the center. They shouldn't be kicked upstairs either. They should be gone. And I think our letters helped. And in fact, that happened. In both these cases, both these teachers left their communities, were asked to leave. In one case, Shimano was asked to leave. Gempo, under the pressure, withdrew himself. And in both cases, there were successor teachers who could step in.

And the national community of Zen teachers expressed support for these successor teachers. And I think that, I don't know how, it must be quite difficult, but I think there's a possibility anyway that the communities could really survive this disaster. This is so much better than years ago when stuff like this would happen. And there was no real support or understandable way of dealing with it. So it was more difficult. Still though, I think that both Shimano and Gempo will continue teaching. Not in those centers, but somehow in other ways. As long as people want to go to them, attracted by their power, they will continue teaching. And no one can really stop them until someone actually takes them to court, which probably will happen at some point.

And take them to court and sue them, and somehow prevent them from continuing. From what I can tell, Shimano is completely unrepentant. I mean, I'm not so close to the situation, but it looks like that. And Gempo seems to be repentant, but one has to be suspicious. Because both these teachers have a long history of this conduct, over more than 25 years. So one can't be naive, as we know. For ourselves, it's hard to change. Very hard to change. So we have to have low expectations and be realistic.

Anyway, actually that's not what I want to talk about today. Because it seems to me that we all know better than this. And I don't think that this sort of thing is something we've ever had to deal with in our sanghas. At least so far. Let's hope for the future that we don't have to deal with it. And I'm pretty sure that if we ever had somebody around in our sanghas, whether it was a teacher or not a teacher, who was this kind of a person, I don't think that that guy would last very long before people were saying to him, well, wait a minute here. Straighten out, buster. You can't be doing this. Certainly the women in our sanghas, I don't think, would be fooled by this for a moment.

So I'm not that worried about it, actually. And I don't so much feel like it's an issue for us, nor do I feel like it's something that I have to comment on or diagnose anybody or condemn anybody. I feel sorry, actually, for everybody involved. So that's not actually what I want to talk about. But I want to talk about something more subtle that this reminds me of, and that's why I bring it up in the beginning. Something that we never talk about because it actually never comes up in the traditional teachings. But it does exist, and it is an important issue for us, and that is gender dynamics in our practice. Now, in talking about this, I'm not trying to say something definitive,

because I think that this is an issue on which there is almost nothing definitive that anybody can say, because no one is free of gender bias. There's nobody outside of gender history looking at it as if they were from Mars. So we're all, you know, prisoners of our conditioning. So I'm not trying to say anything definitive or important other than just to speak about it by way of opening up the subject. And though, as I say, I'm pretty sure that sexual predation is not a big factor in our song of life, probably gender dynamics is, and it's very hard to talk about this stuff, because as soon as you open up your mouth, it stirs deep feelings in all of us.

And we talked about it quite a bit in our song at home in everyday Zen in the Bay Area. We actually had a month of the seminar or so, which we called Women in Buddhism, and we raised these questions and issues of gender. And it was not that easy, it turns out, not so easy. Are you looking for a place to sit? I think there's some spots there in the back. So we had good conversations, and we tried hard, but it was not the most comfortable and happy-making month of our Dharma seminar. At the end, I said at the end, well, how did this go?

And people said, well, I don't know if I liked it that much. But it's not that comfortable to talk about this stuff, actually. It sort of puts all of us on edge. And I don't want to make you feel uncomfortable in what I want to say. And even more than that, I don't want to be uncomfortable. So I'll try to say things that are more on the comfortable side, if possible. So, as many of you here know, Florence Caplow and Sue Moon have been collecting women's Zen and Buddhist stories for a book they're proposing to do.

And they were actually up here in the Northwest doing a weekend, which I think had a big impact that people really enjoyed on those stories. So they've sent me some of the material they have. And I don't know all the stories, but I've looked into this before, and I'm familiar with many of them, and I look forward to looking more closely at their materials. But most of the stories that involve women don't necessarily involve gender issues. You wouldn't know. It doesn't make any difference in a lot of the stories, whether it's a woman or a man.

And that's as it should be. Questions of truth are questions of truth, and it doesn't matter if it's a man or woman or male truth or female truth. It really doesn't matter. But sometimes it does matter. And sometimes we see the difference between a male truth and a female truth. And sometimes through this difference, wider truths emerge. So one of the stories in their collection, which I've seen before, and I don't know, I may have talked about this before,

this particular story really does focus on gender issues. And Every Day's End in the Bay Area also has an annual women's retreat. And this year they focused on this story, and they even dramatized it. They enacted the story. And Chris Forten, one of our senior priests down there, and Sue Moon and others actually played out this koan, this story, like a little drama. So here's the story. Kind of an amazing story, actually.

Wanan was the senior monk at Dahui's monastery. Dahui was a Song dynasty, very famous teacher. And so Song dynasty a little later than most of the stories. Anyway, Wanan was the head monk there, and Dahui had seven women disciples. And Miaozong was the most beautiful of the seven. Miaozong became a nun. But before she became a nun, she would come to practice with Dahui, and he would put her up in the abbot's quarters.

And the head monk Wanan always made disapproving noises about this. And Dahui said to him, even though she is a woman, she has strengths. Wanan did not approve of this at all. So Dahui then insisted that he should interview her. And Wanan didn't want to do it. But finally he agreed. And he sent a message, you know, we'll talk. So Miaozong first said to him,

will this be a Dharma interview or a worldly interview? Wanan replied, a Dharma interview. Miaozong then said to him, then let your attendance go. And she went into the room first. A little moment passed and she said, please come in. When he walked in past the curtain, he saw Miaozong lying face upward on a bed without anything on at all. Naked. Kind of startling.

But Wanan was, you know, a very self-possessed Zen guy. So he walked in, pointed to her genitals and said, what kind of place is this? And Miaozong replied, all the Buddhas of the three worlds and the six patriarchs and all the great monks everywhere come from here. Wanan then said, and would you let me enter or not? Miaozong replied, horses cross, asses cannot cross. This finally left Wanan speechless.

And Miaozong said to him, the interview is over. And she turned over and Wanan, very embarrassed, left the room, went back to Dahui and Dahui said to him, it is certainly not the case that the old dragon does not have any insight. And the story ends, Wanan was ashamed. A pretty provocative story. Miaozong confronts these gender issues head on and nakedly, so to speak. Now it looks like this head monk, Wanan,

unlike our head monk who has been around the block a few times and has some wisdom and seen some things, is not so easily scandalized, I would imagine. But Wanan is easily scandalized or is scandalized. Scandalized by the idea of a woman staying in the monastery in the abbot's quarters. And in reality, these sorts of things that we were talking about in the beginning are not news from yesterday or news from a decade or two ago. There are news from the ages because even in this time in the Song dynasty,

Dahui's teacher, Yuanwu, who was the monk who compiled the Blue Cliff record, he was known to have had many illicit affairs and he would house the women in his monastery. Which is why perhaps Wanan, the head monk, was suspicious of this. So he, I guess, assumes that Miaozong is a woman like that and she has no business being in the monastery. And think about it, maybe if we were around we would be just like him, right? This is wrong, this is scandalous, this is a violation of ethical conduct.

And we too would have been suspicious. But it may be also that Wanan is also beyond worried about ethical conduct, maybe a little prejudiced against women. Maybe he's a little patronizing. How could a woman with a woman's body and a woman's point of view really penetrate the Dharma, he might have thought. He doesn't really want to talk to her about this. He just wants her to go away.

And Dahui realizes that it's much better for him not to defend her but to let her defend herself and she seems more than capable of doing this. So probably, if we're honest, we would have to say that there's no way to pretend when there are men and women involved practicing together, as we do, which when the Japanese see this they cannot imagine how it's possible. Probably there's no way to pretend that when there's men and women together that there's no sexual energy. There's always sexual energy and other kinds of gender-influenced energies,

like fear or resentment. So Wanan knows this and he would like to be protected from it. He would like to remove these energies from the premises, as if he could. And certainly Miaozong could have pleaded with him that she was now a nun, she was now committed to chastity and obedience, and therefore she was no threat to him or any other men in the monastery. She could easily have said that and maybe he would have been satisfied. But that's not what she does.

Instead she confronts the issue with great courage and directness, not apologizing for her feminine body, but emphasizing it. It is this very femininity, this very womb, that is the source of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, she tells him. The feminine in all its starkness is not to be finessed or put up with. It's not a side road, she's telling him, it is the main road. Everyone passes through here. It's wonderful to me that Miaozong fearlessly bears her female body,

as if to say, okay, have a look, this is me. This is the female form with all of its mystery, all of its beauty, and all of its frightfulness. This is what you're afraid of. This is what you doubt. Take a good look. She's saying, it's just me, an ordinary woman. And it's much more than this. It's the Tathagatagarbha, the womb of all the Buddhas, the source of enlightenment, the Buddha nature itself.

That's what Buddha nature is. Tathagatagarbha, which translates literally as womb of all the Buddhas. When we talk about Buddha nature, that's what we're talking about. This womb is the essential heart of our practice. It's what we rely on and have confidence in. The pain of gender is not to be transcended or sidestepped. It itself is the Buddha way. And we sit, we practice hard for three days sitting here,

not to get something we don't have, not to get some relief we're seeking, not to become something that we're not. We sit here because we have confidence in this womb of all the Buddhas, in this Buddha nature. The basic brightness of what we already are, no matter what we are, whether we're a man or a woman, good or bad or skillful or not skillful or good meditators or bad meditators, it makes no difference.

We are alive. We are human. We are embodied as Miaozong is, and we've all come from the great womb of all the Buddhas. And this is most essentially what we are. And this is the mysterious love that sustains us and holds us in its embrace, sitting with confidence in that, returning to that, cutting through our confusion.

That's our practice. This is our zazen. So Miaozong is letting this unfortunately limited head monk know that he should not be denying and protecting himself from what he fears and doesn't understand. She is telling him that this energy, this sexual energy, this energy of gender, this female energy, is essential to true and profound loving-kindness. Without this connecting warmth,

there is no compassion and there is no enlightenment. But unfortunately Mr. Wanan misses this point at the beginning anyway. He must have thought at first that somehow Miaozong is offering herself to him. I was right. He fails to pay attention to what she says to him. He doesn't see the Tathagatagarbha in the body in front of him. Instead he sees what he suspected, the body of an alluring courtesan.

It's not clear to me in the story, probably it doesn't really matter, but it's not clear to me whether Wanan has been so undone by her beauty that he throws his monk's chastity out the window and he actually is dying to have relations with her or whether he's just challenging her in some way. Anyway, you can't fool around with Miaozong. And to Wanan's inquiry, can I enter, she says,

horses cross, asses do not cross. This is a wonderful response, of course. And there's a little background to it, which I'll tell you. It refers to another story that I have to tell you so that you can appreciate. This is a story about Zhaozhou, who I always talk about because I love Zhaozhou. And what I love about him is that he was so unimpressive.

Maybe he's the least impressive of all the Zen masters. Or another way of putting it, he was incredibly impressive, exactly because he was so unimpressive. So it would appear that, from what we know about him, that he was not too charismatic or enlightened. And yet he did become well-known for his teaching. And that's why, in the story I'm about to tell you, a monk travels a far distance to go to visit Zhaozhou.

And he was very unimpressed. It's like disappointing to go really far to see a famous Zen master. And here's this shlomil, you know what I mean? The guy's got nothing going for us. He came a thousand miles, and this is who I'm visiting? So there was a famous bridge in the town where Zhaozhou lived, a famous stone bridge of Zhaozhou. And so speaking in code, the monk says to Zhaozhou,

so I came all this way to see the famous stone bridge of Zhaozhou, but all I see is this old log bridge. Pretty nervy, you know? And Zhaozhou says to him, in a very quiet voice, you can imagine, oh, you see the old log bridge and you don't see the stone bridge. And the monk says, well, what is the stone bridge? The monk's a little bit taken aback by this. He says, well, what is the stone bridge?

And Zhaozhou says, horses cross, asses cross. It's different from what Miaozham says. Horses cross, asses cross. So horses are the great, powerful Zen students, and asses are the not-so-great and not-so-powerful Zen students. So this monk is coming looking for the charismatic, enlightened, powerful Zen master, and with his eyes blinded by that preconception, he fails to see how big and how all-inclusive this practice actually is.

It's not so small as we're looking for this or we're looking for that. It's much bigger than that. And this is just the same what Tim was referring to yesterday in the story of Nanyay. Practice cannot be defiled. It's all-inclusive. It cannot be divided. Yes, it includes the enlightened. That's good. But also it includes the unenlightened. It includes the impressive and also the not-so-impressive

with the recognition that when it comes to Tathagatagarbha, the difference between the enlightened and the unenlightened and the impressive and the not-impressive is like the difference between blue and red, different colors. Maybe red is your favorite color, but you would never go on a campaign against blue or say that blue is of much less value than that. Makes no sense, right?

So the more you're looking for the impressive and the charismatic and the enlightened, the more you may be missing it. And incidentally, or maybe not incidentally, the more vulnerable you may be to your own suffering. So in the story, Maitreya is alluding to this saying of Jaja. And of course she gives it a different twist. She has just demonstrated to one on the all-inclusive nature of her feminine body.

And she shows him that her body is not what one saw and thought it was, a sexualized object tempting to others and limited to itself. The very female form is, as it is, viscerally the Tathagatagarbha, the womb of all Buddhas. All sentient beings are born from this place, asses and horses alike.

And now she makes a further point. Within this limitless feminine form, there are limits. Horses cross, asses don't cross. She's putting our head monk in our proper place, as we could sense, even without knowing the background here. And at the same time, she's affirming the power of consent that goes along with the feminine form. And this is the great sorrow and shame of our species.

Because too often throughout history, and even now, even now in so many places, women have been violently robbed of their consent. They have been raped, they have been demeaned, they have been forced, they have been manipulated into very restricted places. Miao Zong is saying that the true female form cannot be violated that way.

Its power of consent is inherent to it. The womb of the Buddhas issues forth life and shouts its own lion's roar. The nun, Miao Zong, may be open and yielding and all-inclusive, and yet she alone has the power to say, yes, this horse is worthy of me. No, this ass is not. The limitless offering of love and warmth and compassion

also has its proper limits. And ethical precepts obtain, even when we hold them limitlessly in a limitless world, we know the difference between something that can be done and something that should not be done. Miao Zong shows that she has the wisdom and the power to impose those limits herself

when it is correct to do so. So Wan An's worries about her presence in the temple were completely unfounded. She knew exactly why she was there, and she knew exactly how to conduct herself. So I said before that I believe, and I hope it's true, that in our Sangha male sexual predators don't really exist.

And I also hope and believe that narrow-minded, puritanical, possibly misogynistic practitioners don't exist. But these are extremes. Between these extremes there's all sorts of subtle confusions and delusions and hurts and pains about gender. All sorts of ways that probably without any of us intending it, male, unconscious male attitudes are hurtful to women.

And perhaps also it goes the other way around. Women's attitudes are hurtful to men. And probably the reason why we don't speak about it much is that none of us can be quite sure about it. We might have our feelings, but we can't be quite confident that it makes sense to speak of them. And so much of it is unconscious. We all have family histories.

We all have many ways in which we've been conditioned. Some of us have been hurt or dishonored. And despite our best efforts in practice, we can't help but bring our habits and our wounds and our poor training to our daily conduct. And sometimes we feel wounded or we inflict wounds without anybody intending for that to happen. But it does happen.

And it happens pretty much every day. Not only in Zen places. It would be nice if it could be restricted to Zen places. And then we could say, bring it all here. We'll suffer. Unfortunately, it's not restricted to Zen places. It's everywhere. And I think we all have to realize that we are very lucky here.

Because in the world that we live in, it's so shockingly different in other parts of the world. And this is, I think, one of the cultural battlegrounds of world culture right now. But here, it's not so restrictive and so difficult. There is not what we would call terrible, serious and violent oppression of women here. And of gay and lesbian people.

All people, all genders and races. We don't have that so much here. By and large, at least by comparison, we have an equal chance. And we are all accorded respect. And it's the law here. It's a blessing. It's the law.

And little by little, it becomes more and more the social custom. And even here, we're still having our battles over the law and the custom. But even so, there's plenty of hurt and pain. Plenty of confusion. And even when all the hurt and pain is gone, and all the laws provide everyone

with freedom and equality, we'll still have the long history of all of this to deal with. And we try our best to bring to awareness what we are unaware of and to follow through our commitment to benefit rather than hurt each other. In our Soto Zen way of practice,

especially in the everyday Zen way, we emphasize warm human relationships. We emphasize deep trust and mutual commitment. And we honor and give power to senior practitioners. And I think this is a good thing. This is the way that we've inherited, and I think it's a good way.

And I personally prefer it to some other way in which what's given credit and power is accomplishment or brilliance or social connection or polish. Our way is very simple and very warm-hearted. If you practice, we honor you. We respect you. We love you. Our way is a way of love.

We grow to accept and love one another in the Dharma as we go forward practicing together, as we were saying yesterday. We practiced together a long time. We appreciate each other. We accept each other. We know our foibles, and we don't deny it,

but we accept and appreciate. But with this emphasis on love and relationship, there may also be some problems. People who love one another can misunderstand one another and even hurt one another without intending to do that. And I know that sometimes

women have complained about me and other of our male leaders as not really understanding sometimes what a woman is feeling or saying. I have felt maybe that I misinterpreted or misunderstood or didn't appreciate what is said or what is indicated. And sometimes women have complained about me

or other senior male students saying something or doing something, some word or gesture that maybe in the grand scheme of things is not so bad, but to that person did really matter and was hurtful. And maybe once or twice we've misunderstood

one another so that it seems as if inappropriate relationships are being fostered. So probably lots of stuff like this is happening all the time. And we're all, I think, trying to deal with it the best we can. And I think we're doing pretty good.

I think we're pretty mature and understanding and aware people. And I would say that we're doing well. And I don't believe that I have a problem or we have a problem or our other senior teachers have a problem. At least this is my hope. I hope this is right.

Somebody after this talk will let me know. I'm sure I'll hear about that. That's one reason why I'm saying it. I'm letting you know that I want to hear about it if that's not the case. That's what I believe anyway. And I'm pretty sure that if I do have a problem

or others of us have a problem, that someone will eventually let me or us know. And that we will find a way to deal with it that is open-minded and compassionate. We don't have to be afraid of problems. And it would be very bad if we were afraid to bring up something

that seemed wrong or troubling to us, even if just troubling to me, troubling to an individual. We need to feel that we can bring it up. Now, saying that, I also hasten to say that it would also be fine if you have something
that you could easily let go. Please let it go. Because it would be a rough world if we were all the time, each one of us, letting each other know about all the things that we were saying and doing

that were somewhat less than perfectly thoughtful. I can imagine that if we took up a practice like this, we would have no time to sit. We would have to spend three days in deep conversation about reviewing yesterday's conversation.

So I guess one could take this all too far. But still, if it would be good for us, if it would be good for me, and any of our senior teachers, educational for us, to sometimes discuss these things so that we could understand better the different gender dynamics,

this would be worthwhile, I think. Now, the usual way that this is framed is, and I've heard this many times, and I don't really disagree, men are so clueless. They really have no interest in and no capacity for feeling anything, whereas women are so much more sensitive
and see so much more. And this may very well be true. But also, it may insufficiently take into account the inevitable gender bias that women have. However they come by it, they may have that.

So I think the conversation always begins with the realization that we're all a little bit off. That's what it means to be human with six senses. It means you're always going to be a little bit off, everyone in our own special way,

a little bit off. So I'll conclude with some words from Chris, who I was telling you, some of you know Chris Fortin, who she actually, she said she did not take off all her clothes to enact this. She put on a body stocking, she said.

Very, very resourceful. But at the Women's Retreat, and she said that enacting that koan, putting her sort of body into that koan had a big impact on her. She's still sort of trying to sort out what it meant to her. It was a big deal for her.

And she gave a talk about it at the Women's Retreat, so I'll end my talk today with quoting a few paragraphs from her talk. So this is Chris's words. The theme for the Every Day Zen Women's Weekend is authentic meeting, ferocious vulnerability.

And Tim was talking quite a bit yesterday about this important study on vulnerability. And that's what they use as a theme for their retreat. Vulnerable ferocity. The dictionary offers us this about the source of these words. Ferocious denotes wild.

Vulnerable is capable of being physically or emotionally wounded, completely seen. That's interesting, huh? Capable of being physically or emotionally wounded, completely seen. Miao Zhang was naked in this encounter. Nakedness means unarmed,

without addition or concealment. Nothing extra. Bare. On reflection, this seems to express the heart of the practice that we share with Miao Zhang and all of our ancestors. Zazen becomes the naked, unarmed,
